item.title: Cross-Platform Cloud Benchmark Reveals Wide Gap Between Physical Qubit Counts and Entangled GHZ State Sizes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article underscores a stark reality: even the largest publicly‑available superconducting processors can only generate GHZ states spanning a tiny fraction of their physical qubits when run without error mitigation. By benchmarking nine cloud platforms with identical workflows, the study quantifies how far current hardware is from delivering high‑fidelity multipartite entanglement—a prerequisite for many quantum algorithms and error‑correction schemes. The findings dovetail with recent pushes toward better calibration, noise‑aware compilation, and mitigation techniques, reminding readers that raw qubit counts alone are not yet a reliable metric of usable quantum power.

A new study benchmarked nine cloud-accessible quantum processors, revealing a significant gap between the number of physical qubits and the size of entangled GHZ states achievable without error mitigation. The research, which utilized standard remote cloud workflows, found that large superconducting processors only maintain multipartite entanglement across a small fraction of their physical registers. This highlights the challenges in achieving high-fidelity multipartite entanglement in current quantum hardware. item.title: Real-time simulation of scattering in $φ^4$ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a core obstacle in quantum‑field‑theory simulations by presenting a scalable way to prepare localized wave packets directly from the interacting vacuum, which is essential for realistic scattering experiments on quantum hardware. It extends recent variational and Lorentz‑symmetry techniques to ensure that the prepared states converge correctly in the continuum limit, offering clear diagnostics of Airy‑type distortions and their mitigation as lattice spacing is refined. The work gives practitioners concrete guidance on parameter regimes for reliable two‑particle scattering studies, a step forward as experimental groups target small‑scale φ⁴ simulations on superconducting or trapped‑ion platforms. Nonetheless, the observed artificial inelasticity from coarse digitization highlights that finer field encoding and error mitigation will still be required for quantitatively accurate results.

Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in $φ^4$ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulation of scattering.

item.title: Complex fluid flow dynamics by bright scattershot boson sampling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a photonic boson‑sampling device can be repurposed as a high‑dimensional analog processor for simulating nonlinear fluid dynamics, extending the scattershot approach to “bright” regimes that harvest every generated photon number pattern. By demonstrating accurate forecasts of an eight‑parameter convection model and a 16‑parameter atmospheric circulation model—while tolerating up to 50 % loss—the work positions boson sampling as a competitive alternative to classical reservoir computers for time‑series prediction. The result bridges fundamental quantum optics with practical sensing and modeling tasks, suggesting that near‑term photonic hardware could accelerate complex flow simulations without requiring full fault‑tolerant quantum computers. However, the performance gains are currently demonstrated in simulation, so experimental validation will be key to confirming scalability beyond the digital twin.

Boson sampling machines have become a fruitful tool for establishing new concepts, which connect fundamental physics with computer science applications. Here, we exploit the intrinsically high-dimensional correlations generated by the measurement outcomes of a multiphoton boson sampling machine and demonstrate how a reconfigurable architecture can be programmed to autonomously model the time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems that describe complex fluid flows. By extending on the original scattershot boson sampling (SBS) scheme to include higher photon number components -- a scheme which we label bright scattershot boson sampling (BSBS) --- this scheme overcomes scaling issues inherent to SBS-based schemes by utilizing all randomly generated input photon number distributions. We illustrate the capability of this scheme for two complex fluid-flow models: an eight-dimensional Lorenz-type model of two-dimensional thermally driven convection and a 16-dimensional model of global atmospheric circulation. Using a digital twin of the BSBS architecture based on multiphoton statistics, we show that the photonic approach accurately reproduces the temporal dynamics of both systems while being resilient to photon losses of up to 50 per cent. We also verified that the BSBS case outperforms a comparable run with coherent light. Moreover, its prediction horizon exceeds that of a classical reservoir-computing model with the same query complexity. These results highlight the potential of near-term photonic quantum computing for addressing relevant real-world tasks on noisy intermediate-scale devices.

item.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a large‑language‑model agent can automatically synthesize fault‑tolerant Clifford circuits across a suite of logical‑code tasks, turning what has been a painstaking hand‑crafted process into an evolvable program‑generation pipeline. By coupling the model’s pretrained knowledge with a rigorous circuit verifier, the approach delivers verified, exhaustive fault‑coverage for state preparation, gate design and code‑switching—capabilities that have only recently begun to be explored with machine learning in quantum compilation. If the method scales to larger codes and non‑Clifford operations, it could dramatically shorten the hardware‑software co‑design cycle needed to bring truly error‑corrected quantum processors toward practical advantage.

Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

item.title: Solution of the Qubit Marginal Problem from Fermionic Representability
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first exact solution of the qubit marginal problem by translating it into fermionic representability, a move that bridges two traditionally separate formalisms and unlocks powerful N‑representability hierarchies for ordinary qubits. By showing that low‑order positivity constraints already capture the ground‑state physics of frustrated Heisenberg and transverse‑field Ising chains to sub‑percent accuracy, it offers a practical, analytically tractable tool for both classical simulation and error mitigation on near‑term quantum hardware. The result positions marginal‑compatibility checks as a new diagnostic layer for quantum processors, though its effectiveness beyond one‑dimensional spin models remains an open question.

Whether local reduced states are compatible with a global quantum state---the quantum marginal problem---is central to quantum information and simulation. Here we present a solution to the ensemble marginal problem for qubits based on the representability theory of fermions. Encoding each qubit as one fermion in two orbitals, we prove that the representable qubit marginals form an exposed face of the set of $N$-representable fermionic reduced density matrices, selected by the vanishing of every site-occupation variance. Complete hierarchies of fermionic representability conditions therefore transfer exactly to qubits. Applications to frustrated Heisenberg and transverse-field Ising rings show that the $(2,3)$-positivity conditions are exact at the Majumdar--Ghosh point and accurate to about 0.5% at criticality. Because the conditions hold for any quantum state, they also provide a framework for mitigating measurement errors on qubit-based quantum devices.

item.title: Dissipation as a Resource for Entanglement via High-Spin Mediator Purification
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that engineered dissipation can actively purify a thermally mixed high‑spin impurity and turn it into a powerful entangling bus, achieving a negativity of 0.64 at 12 K—far above the temperatures where most solid‑state spin qubits retain coherence. By demonstrating a non‑monotonic optimum pump rate, the work links recent advances in optical pumping of magnetic atoms to practical hardware designs that exploit rather than suppress decoherence channels. The result suggests a new route to robust two‑qubit gates in impurity‑based platforms, though scaling will require careful management of the same dissipative coupling that delivers the entanglement.

We study entanglement generation between two spin qubits mediated by a single, thermally mixed, high-spin ($S=5/2$) magnetic impurity, using the Lindblad master equation to compare coherent and dissipative control of the mediator. We show that no coherent drive, however strong or resonant, can purify the mediator beyond its thermal value --- a direct consequence of unitary evolution exactly preserving state purity --- while a dissipative channel purifies it up to the limit set by the optical pumping cycle itself, $\mathrm{Tr}[ρ_M^2]\approx0.8$. Modeling this channel with rates fixed by the measured optical pumping of a single Mn spin, we find that the entanglement it enables is not monotonic in the pump strength: it peaks at a finite rate and then decreases, since the same channel leaks decoherence to the qubits through the coupling that mediates their entanglement. At the experimental pumping rate, a single $80$ns pulse purifies the mediator, the resulting polarization persists for a timescale three orders of magnitude longer than the entangling dynamics, and the first-recurrence negativity rises from $0.18$ to $0.64$ at $12$K, remaining above $0.6$ up to $30$K. These results establish dissipation, not as noise to be suppressed, but as the very resource that makes robust entanglement generation possible.

item.title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it tackles the long‑standing data‑loading bottleneck by showing how to map thousands of classical values directly onto a quantum processor without any SWAP routing, leveraging the native coupling graph of the hardware. By extending earlier QPIXL and QCrank ideas into a checkerboard layout that pairs address and data qubits, Tessa demonstrates scalable state preparation on IBM’s Phoenix and Fez devices—an advance that could accelerate near‑term quantum‑machine‑learning and quantum‑simulation workflows. The approach is still constrained by readout noise and the degree of local connectivity, but it proves that device‑aware encoding can be realized today on real hardware.

We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to $1568$ real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data. Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits. When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree. As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.

item.title: Chip-Based Discrete-Modulated Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution with Uncertainty-Principle-Based Composable Security
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that high‑order discrete‑modulated continuous‑variable QKD can be secured with a tight, uncertainty‑principle‑based composable analysis, eliminating the heavy numerical overhead that has hampered practical finite‑size proofs. By streamlining the security evaluation to essentially one‑dimensional searches—and even an analytical bound—the authors enable real‑time key generation at 17 Mbps on a discrete‑component platform and over half a megabit per second on a silicon‑photonic receiver across 50 km of fiber, a clear milestone for integrated telecom‑compatible quantum cryptography. The work bridges the gap between laboratory‑grade CV‑QKD demonstrations and deployable, chip‑scale secure communication systems, though further optimisation will be needed to bring silicon‑based rates up to parity with bulk optics.

Continuous-variable quantum key distribution offers a promising platform for scalable quantum networks through its compatibility with standard telecommunications technology and photonic integration. High-order discrete modulation facilitates practical implementation while approaching the key-rate performance of ideal Gaussian modulation, but its finite-size composable security analysis entails substantial computational overhead. Here, we develop an uncertainty-principle-based security framework that enables finite-size composable key-rate evaluation against collective attacks for constellations up to 256-QAM. By introducing a heterodyne-measured ancillary mode into the entanglement-based source description, we incorporate additional source correlations into the security analysis that allow the Heisenberg uncertainty principle alone to provide a tight bound for the unknown correlations in a covariance matrix characterizing the whole system. Matrix symmetrization further reduces the key-rate optimization to a one-dimensional search, while subsequent mode reduction yields an analytical lower bound requiring no numerical search. Experimental demonstrations using 256-QAM on discrete-component and silicon-photonic-receiver platforms achieve finite-size composable secret key rates of 17.436 and 0.519 Mbps, respectively, over a 50 km fiber link. This approach facilitates the practical deployment of high-speed, real-time and compact quantum key distribution systems. Beyond quantum key distribution, the principle of tightening uncertainty-constrained bounds via source-mode expansion offers a paradigm for exploring the information-theoretic properties of complex non-Gaussian systems.

item.title: Observing Enhanced Entanglement in an Ising Quantum Register Beyond Weak Measurement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by tailoring a periodic‑measurement pattern one can dramatically boost the entanglement that survives after a projective readout of an Ising‑coupled register—something previously thought to be exponentially unlikely in noisy devices. The protocol bridges recent work on measurement‑induced phase transitions and matrix‑product‑state simulations, offering a concrete recipe for experimentally accessing highly entangled post‑measurement states without excessive overhead. If the scaling ansatz holds for larger processors, it could become a practical tool for enhancing quantum sensing and error‑mitigation schemes that rely on strong multipartite correlations.

Measurements often yield a disentangled quantum state which is the most probable measurement outcome while the measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement could be exponentially less probable or absent. Higher probability in measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement is virtue in experimental observation of enhance entanglement in post-selected or Born-rule measurements with less resources in noisy quantum devices. We develop a periodic measurement sampling(PMS) protocol in the framework of uniform matrix product states. item.title: Fer expansion converges almost twice as far as Magnus for qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the Fer series—an alternative to the widely used Magnus expansion for simulating time‑dependent qubit dynamics—has a provably larger convergence radius, roughly twice as large as the universal Magnus bound of π. The Fer expansion writes the propagator of a time-dependent Hamiltonian as a product of unitary exponentials whose error decreases doubly exponentially with the number of factors, while the Magnus expansion improves by one order at a time. This is almost twice the optimal universal Magnus threshold $π$; the bound on a single Fer step is sharp, while the exact convergence radius remains open.

In the interesting case of a bipartite Hilbert space of unequal prime dimensions, $\mathcal{H}_p\otimes\mathcal{H}_q$, with $p<q$ prime, the standard solution provides $p+1$ product bases. item.title: Entropic quantum error correction for independent and correlated amplitude damping errors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that entropic quantum error‑correction can be implemented analytically with only 2×2 unitaries, turning a previously intractable matrix problem into a handful of elementary linear‑algebra steps. By exploiting structures in the quantum conditional mutual information, the authors produce simple, explicit recovery maps for both independent and correlated amplitude‑damping errors that achieve near‑optimal entanglement fidelity while requiring far less computational overhead than conventional global decoders. The result is especially noteworthy because it provides one of the first practical, low‑complexity solutions for correlated damping—a regime where few short‑code techniques exist—potentially easing the resource burden for near‑term quantum devices. Readers should note that worst‑case fidelity still lags the absolute theoretical optimum by about 9 percent, but the trade‑off in simplicity and scalability makes the approach highly relevant to current error‑mitigation efforts.

The idea of using quantum entropy for quantum error correction (QEC) has existed for a long time. However, its computational complexity has limited its practical use: even a $[[4,1]]$ code for standard independent amplitude damping errors involves a $256\times 256$ Hermitian matrix, so the approach scales poorly as the codeword length increases. For correlated errors, the situation is even worse. In this paper, we show that, by using the insights developed in our previous paper and exploiting certain structures of quantum conditional mutual information, we can solve these problems exactly by hand, using only $2\times 2$ unitary matrices. By examining the entropy, we identify the leakage channels and the amount of leakage exactly, then define the recovery map accordingly. The rules defining our recovery map are simple, intuitive, and computationally inexpensive: for independent errors, it is based on 16 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions; for correlated errors, it is based on 6 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions. Our method sacrifices little in terms of performance: for the widely used entanglement fidelity, our simple QEC recovery map achieves a sharp result; for the worst-case fidelity, the best result is about $9\%$ better than ours; for correlated errors, there are no comparable results for short codewords. Among the known techniques, our recovery map is the first non-global one. The calculations use elementary linear algebra and calculus, and is presented in great detail.

item.description:

Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

item.description:

Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under $\hat{S}^2$, and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.

item.title: Max-Cut QAOA on Non-Hardware-Native Graphs via MinLA Surrogates and Configuration Recovery
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a key bottleneck for near‑term QAOA implementations by showing how to prune long‑range edges in non‑native MAX‑CUT graphs and then recover lost objective value with lightweight classical post‑processing. By leveraging a Minimum Linear Arrangement ordering to keep only short‑distance two‑qubit gates, the authors dramatically cut SWAP overhead on devices like IBM Kingston while still achieving competitive cuts after signed‑residue or bipartite‑block recovery. The workflow dovetails with recent hardware‑aware compilation and hybrid quantum–classical strategies, offering a practical path to scale QAOA to larger, irregular graphs without demanding deeper circuits. For non-hardware-native \textsc{MAX-CUT} instances, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can incur additional two-qubit depth overhead due to SWAP-based routing of interactions between non-adjacent qubits. We propose a hybrid quantum--classical workflow that reduces this depth by selectively removing interactions and subsequently recovers solution quality through classical optimization of the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective. We employ a Minimum Linear Arrangement (MinLA)-based vertex ordering to preferentially retain short-range interactions, thereby constructing a two-qubit depth-reduced surrogate QAOA ansatz. To compensate for the information lost through interaction removal, we develop classical \textit{recovery} strategies that refine QPU-sampled bitstrings directly on the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective. We develop two recovery strategies: signed-residue-based local search and bipartite-block optimization, where each conditional block problem is solved exactly using an $s$--$t$ minimum cut. Recovery is performed independently on each sampled configuration, ensuring monotonic improvement in cut value without additional QPU executions. We evaluate the workflow on \texttt{ibm\_kingston} for 120 distinct non-hardware-native instances comprising $6$-regular and Erdős--Rényi graphs with 40, 60 and 100 vertices. We verify that the surrogates substantially reduce transpiled two-qubit depth while staying within the prescribed two-qubit depth, and with recovery yield \textit{near-optimal} cuts on the original graphs. These results demonstrate the potential of hardware-aware interaction selection and classical recovery to extend QAOA to graph instances whose full cost Hamiltonians exceed practical circuit-depth budgets.

This book introduces quantum electromagnetics to readers trained in classical electromagnetics, without assuming a systematic background in quantum mechanics. The central question is when classical descriptions suffice, and when the quantum states of matter or the field must be retained explicitly. Starting from familiar electromagnetic modes and material response, the discussion develops atomic dynamics, field quantization, and the interaction of quantized fields with quantum matter. The final discussion examines how sensitivity and claims of quantum advantage depend on bandwidth, measurement resources, and the classical reference used for comparison. The aim is to help readers choose an appropriate model, carry out the calculation, and understand what its predictions mean for an electromagnetic measurement.

item.description:

Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretically secure key sharing between two distant parties. Recently, one promising QKD protocol which can distribute a secret key over long distances called twin-field QKD (TF-QKD) has been developed. However, it requires active compensation for experimental imperfections such as phase, polarization, and frequency fluctuations with expensive devices and this makes its experimental implementation challenging. Here, we propose a long-distance continuous-variable QKD (CV-QKD) protocol which is inspired by TF-QKD. Our protocol can remove these requirements by using Gaussian-modulated coherent states and digital signal processing which is widely used in recent digital coherent optical communication and experimental implementations of CV-QKD. For security analysis, we use a numerical optimization approach with a photon-number cutoff assumption. We propose a new set of constraints for numerical optimization which can efficiently constrain a highly non-Gaussian quantum state shared by two legitimate parties in our protocol. We show that the key rate of our protocol exceeds the key rate of a direct-transmission CV-QKD protocol at long distances and it can overcome the repeaterless bound.

This score allows processors with different coupling topologies to be compared on a common scale and can inform the design of coupling topologies for scalable chips.

The universal properties of state ensembles generated by quantum dynamics provide a refined lens into Hilbert-space ergodicity and deep thermalisation, or lack thereof. We investigate deep-ergodicity breaking transitions of an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing dynamics via hybrid quantum circuits, where unitary evolution is interspersed with projective measurements. Specifically, we analyse the statistical properties of two distinct state ensembles: the trajectory ensemble (TE) conditioned on the measurement outcomes of the hybrid circuit, and the projected ensemble (PE) generated by further projective measurements of the system at the final temporal boundary. We find that both ensembles undergo non-analytic changes -- ensemble phase transitions -- at the critical point of the measurement-induced purification transition, despite their first moments remaining completely maximally mixed and blind to the transition. For Haar-random circuits, the TE transitions from a trivial identity ensemble to the uniform Haar ensemble, while the PE transitions from the Haar ensemble to a trivial singleton pure state. In Clifford circuits, absence of non-stabiliserness limits the PE to a $1$-design, while the TE forms a $k$-design for $k \leq 3$. We demonstrate that these genuine ensemble transitions offer a clear physical mechanism for the measurement-induced entanglement or purification transitions, illustrating how the capacity to ergodically steer a quantum subsystem shifts from the temporal boundary measurements in the mixed phase to the bulk trajectory measurements in the pure phase.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) generates shared secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. We report the entanglement-based segment of the Slovak national quantum communication infrastructure, connecting four cities in western Slovakia over deployed telecommunication fiber. Polarization-entangled photons generated at a central node are passively routed by wavelength to form a trusted-node-free, fully meshed sub-network of three cities, with the fourth connected through the central node and all links operated simultaneously. Unlike most previous demonstrations, which estimate key rates from raw coincidences, all rates reported here are obtained after the complete post-processing chain, with keys delivered in real time via ETSI GS QKD 014. With partial non-local chromatic dispersion compensation, we obtain 13.5 bit/s over 109 km, and 4.3 bit/s over 32.1 dB of accumulated loss between two cities without a direct fiber link. Benchmarking against finite-key security bounds shows that the implemented heuristic privacy amplification can exceed the finite-key bound, and that replacing detect-and-discard with error correction would increase the finite-key rate by a factor of 4.1-6.6, and yield a positive finite-key rate on the 142.9 km link where the implemented scheme yields none.

item.title: Implementation of a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD under finite-size parameter estimation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first fully integrated experimental demonstration of a one‑dimensional Gaussian‑modulated CV‑QKD system using independent lasers and a local‑local oscillator, achieving a privacy‑amplified key rate of 1.421 Mbit/s (asymptotic) and 0.364 Mbit/s when finite‑size effects are included over 12 km of standard fiber. By simplifying the modulation to a single quadrature while still delivering megabit‑per‑second rates, it addresses long‑standing hardware complexity concerns and brings continuous‑variable QKD closer to practical telecom deployment. The results also highlight that finite‑size parameter estimation remains a bottleneck, underscoring the need for larger data blocks or more efficient reconciliation to reach commercial‑grade performance.

Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising technology for quantum-secure communications, offering high secret-key rates and straightforward integration with coherent optical communication systems. Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, increasing requirements for state preparation, modulation, and calibration, while potentially introducing additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional (1D) Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, while the conjugate quadrature constrains the protocol's security. However, an integrated experimental 1D implementation combining independent-laser coherent reception with practical reconciliation, finite-size parameter estimation, and privacy amplification remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD system over 12~km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator (LLO) architecture with independent lasers and an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. The implementation includes coherent detection, digital signal processing, information reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification. The 1D system achieves a privacy-amplified rate of $1.421$~Mbit/s under the asymptotic security treatment and $0.364$~Mbit/s under the finite-size scenario. These results establish an experimental baseline for the performance--complexity trade-off associated with unidimensional Gaussian modulation and provide an experimental basis for developing lower-complexity CV-QKD transmitters.

item.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a frozen, general‑purpose large language model can directly suggest full parameter sets for variational quantum circuits, offering a shortcut to the costly classical optimization loop that underpins most VQE workflows. The study finds the shortcut works best when the target Hamiltonian exhibits recognizable physical or mathematical structure—such as molecular or parent‑Hamiltonian problems—while it struggles on generic random instances and gains little from iterative feedback. By highlighting both the promise of AI‑driven circuit initialization for structured quantum chemistry tasks and its current limits, the work helps steer future hybrid approaches toward problems where problem‑specific patterns can be leveraged.

Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

item.title: Explicit Absolutely Maximally Entangled states in dimensions twice a prime power
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first explicit families of absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states in local dimensions that are twice an odd prime power, closing a long‑standing gap in multipartite entanglement constructions and completing the nine‑party AME classification for all integer dimensions ≥ 3. By coupling qubits with higher‑dimensional q‑level systems, the authors obtain scalable AME(N, 2q) states that can be directly translated into optimal quantum error‑correcting codes and secret‑sharing schemes, a development that dovetails with recent advances in high‑dimensional quantum networking and holographic code design. The work also highlights an exponential growth requirement on q for larger N, underscoring both the power of the new construction and the remaining challenge of finding more resource‑efficient AME states.

Absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states are pure multipartite states with maximally mixed reductions on every set of at most half the parties. We construct explicit families in local dimension $2q$, twice an odd prime power $q$, using an established coupling of qubits and $q$-level systems. The $q$-level states remove interference between branches, so the qubit states need maximally mixed reductions only on average. This gives AME$(9,2q)$ and AME$(11,2q)$ for every odd prime power $q\geq5$, AME$(13,2q)$ for $q\geq17$, AME$(15,2q)$ for $q\geq9$, and AME$(17,2q)$ for $q\geq67$. For every odd $N\geq3$, the same coupling gives AME$(N,2q)$ under the sufficient condition $q\geq\max\{N,2^{N-2}\}$ on the odd prime power $q$. Within this coupling, the smallest such $q$ must grow exponentially with $N$. Combined with known inputs and products, these families complete the nine-party classification: for integer $d\geq2$, an AME$(9,d)$ state exists if and only if $d\geq3$. Choosing the branch pairing also gives AME$(15,2p)$ states with a cyclic shift of the parties compensated by local unitaries, for every prime $p\equiv1\pmod{15}$.

item.title: Noise robust super-Heisenberg scaling in time-dependent quantum sensing by subspace-twirled dynamical decoupling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that subspace‑twirled dynamical decoupling can preserve the signal of a time‑dependent Hamiltonian while canceling environmental noise, thereby delivering super‑Heisenberg scaling without the heavy overhead of adaptive control. By proving rigorous conditions under which the twirling protocol works, the authors bridge a gap between idealized quantum metrology proposals and realistic sensor hardware that must contend with decoherence. If experimentally realized, the technique could simplify the construction of ultraprecise magnetic or frequency sensors, although practical implementation will still need to verify the assumed noise models and control fidelity.

In quantum parameter estimation, time-dependent Hamiltonians can enable ultraprecise estimates of a physical parameter beyond the standard Heisenberg limit, also called the super-Heisenberg limit. However, achieving optimal scaling of the measurement precision typically requires an adaptive quantum control scheme which is resource-intensive and hard to implement in general. Furthermore, this advantage is often severely eroded by environmental noise. We propose the use of a dynamical decoupling scheme based on subspace twirling -- the averaging of random unitaries over a subspace rather than the entire Hilbert space -- to overcome these two limitations. We first prove necessary and sufficient conditions for subspace twirling to preserve the encoding signal while simultaneously removing environmental noise. We then establish conditions and provide performance guarantees for when time dependent Hamiltonians undergoing subspace twirling can achieve super-Heisenberg scaling without adaptive controls. Finally, we illustrate our results using an explicit example where a qubit sensor undergoing a subspace twirl simultaneously suppresses noise and achieves super-Heisenberg scaling. These results offer guidance for the design of ultraprecise quantum sensors under time-dependent and noisy conditions.

item.title: Entanglement detection from moments of the realigned state: application to continuous-variable quantum systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a practical entanglement‑witness that sidesteps full continuous‑variable tomography by measuring second‑order moments of the realigned density operator, an approach that can be implemented with a linear interferometer acting on multiple copies of the state. It builds directly on the recent multicopy techniques used to access partial‑transpose moments (Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033064 2026) and shows that even modest experimental resources suffice to certify entanglement in both Gaussian and highly non‑Gaussian states such as lossy NOON states. By providing a scalable, experimentally friendly tool, the work could accelerate verification of quantum‑optical platforms where full state reconstruction is prohibitive.

Certifying entanglement is a central problem in quantum information sciences, especially for continuous-variable quantum systems where full state tomography is experimentally demanding. We introduce a family of separability criteria based on the singular moments and weak moments of the operator obtained by applying the realignment map to the density operator. In practice, we find that the criterion based on the second-order moments of the realigned operator is already sufficient to witness the entanglement of a wide range of quantum optical states. The realigned moments can be readily accessed using an optical scheme consisting of a linear interferometer that couples several identical copies of the state, similarly to the multicopy technique used to measure the partial-transpose moments of a state [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033064 (2026)]. We illustrate the detection capability of the second-order realigned-moment method for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, including lossy NOON states.
